question:
Patient note:
A 73-year-old man was evaluated this afternoon on the orthopedic surgery ward in preparation for a scheduled left total knee replacement that is set to take place tomorrow morning under general anesthesia and a femoral nerve block; the operative team anticipates a three-hour procedure with at least several days of inpatient recovery. The forthcoming joint reconstruction is the latest step in management of end-stage tricompartmental osteoarthritis that has limited his ability to stand for more than a few minutes over the past year. Three weeks ago he underwent a laparoscopic sigmoid resection for complicated diverticulitis at this same hospital, an operation that lasted just over four hours and required two postoperative nights on the surgical floor before discharge; he recovered uneventfully from that abdominal procedure. Unfortunately, one week after going home he slipped while descending his porch steps, landing awkwardly on his left leg and sustaining a minimally displaced lateral tibial plateau fracture confirmed by plain radiographs and CT scan. Because the articular surface remained congruent, the fracture was treated non-operatively with protected weight bearing in a hinged neoprene brace rather than a hard cast. Since that fall he has been largely confined to his bedroom recliner or bed, getting up only with assistance to use the bedside commode, and nursing documentation shows fewer than 50 feet of ambulation in the last four days; he notes that any attempt to move around causes immediate knee pain that he fears will worsen the fracture. He denies fevers, shakes, night sweats, purulent sputum, dysuria, or abdominal discomfort since the colectomy, and recalls no recent episodes of systemic infection. Review of systems is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, new ankle swelling, exertional chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or transient neurologic deficit. He has a long history of tobacco-related chronic bronchitis; although he quit cigarettes 10 years ago after a 45-pack-year exposure, he still uses a twice-daily long-acting muscarinic inhaler and keeps a rescue albuterol inhaler nearby for intermittent wheeze but has not required oral steroids or emergency visits this year. He has never experienced clot formation in the legs or lungs, and none of his close relatives has been treated for a thrombotic event. He recalls receiving unfractionated heparin only during prior surgeries without any unexplained drop in platelet counts, and no physician has ever advised him of an underlying blood-clotting disorder. Other chronic conditions include diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and well-managed hypertension; there is no personal history of cancer, inflammatory bowel illness, myocardial infarction, or peripheral vascular disease. Current medications are tiotropium, albuterol as needed, lisinopril 10 mg daily, acetaminophen-hydrocodone for pain, and a multivitamin; he takes no hormone therapy, steroids, anticoagulants, or anti-platelet agents other than baby aspirin, which was held yesterday per orthopedic protocol. Socially, he lives with his spouse in a single-story home, used to garden regularly, drinks a glass of wine on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. On examination he is resting supine in an adjustable hospital bed, conversant and oriented. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, pulse 84/min and regular, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 95 % on room air. He is slender with body mass index 23 kg/m² and breathes comfortably without accessory muscle use. Cardiovascular assessment reveals a normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation with slightly prolonged expiratory phase but no crackles or rhonchi. Abdomen is soft and non-tender; a well-healed 5-cm infra-umbilical trocar scar is noted without hernia or incisional pain. The left lower extremity is encased in a black hinged brace locked at 30 degrees; gentle palpation along the lateral tibial plateau produces mild discomfort but there is no warmth, erythema, or swelling, and calf circumference is symmetric to the right side. Skin of both legs is warm and well perfused, without discoloration, varicosities, or pitting edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally. Sensory and motor testing show intact light touch and full strength of ankle dorsiflexion, though knee extension is limited by pain. There is no peripherally inserted central catheter or other indwelling vascular device; two 20-gauge peripheral IVs placed yesterday remain patent in the forearm. Neurologic examination is nonfocal. Laboratory results obtained two hours ago reveal hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, platelet count 247 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.3 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, glucose 108 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, and a baseline coagulation profile of PT 12.3 s (INR 1.0) and aPTT 30 s. Electrocardiogram records normal sinus rhythm at 82 bpm with nonspecific ST-T wave changes unchanged from previous tracings. Upright chest radiograph shows hyperinflated lungs consistent with his chronic bronchitis but no acute infiltrate or effusion. Pulmonary function tests from last year demonstrated an FEV₁ of 62 % predicted without significant bronchodilator response. The anesthesia service has deemed his airway Mallampati class II, and he tolerates lying flat without desaturation. He has had nothing by mouth since midnight, and no mechanical or pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has yet been initiated as the peri-operative plan is still being finalized by the surgical team in conjunction with medicine and anesthesia.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds points for distinct perioperative risk factors:
- Age 73 (61–74 years): 2.
- Scheduled elective total knee replacement: 5. Do not also count it as generic major surgery.
- Separate major operation within the past month (four-hour colectomy three weeks ago): 1.
- Recent leg fracture (tibial plateau): 5. The hinged brace is not a plaster cast.
- Confinement to bed or chair for more than 72 hours, with only assisted commode trips: 2.
- Chronic obstructive lung disease documented by chronic bronchitis and obstructive spirometry: 1.
Total = 2 + 5 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 16.
Final answer: 16
